doc.title: async-http-clients.md
doc.content:
# Timeouts and Connection Pooling in Async HTTP Clients

## Overview

An async HTTP client separates the *transport* (sockets, TLS, connection reuse)
from the *request lifecycle* (build a request, send it, stream a response back).
Most timeout bugs in production services come from configuring one of those two
layers while assuming you configured the other.

## The four timeouts

A single "timeout" number is almost always wrong, because four different
operations can hang independently:

- **Connect timeout.** How long to wait for a TCP connection (and TLS handshake)
  to a host that may be unreachable. Typical production value: 3 to 5 seconds.
  A long connect timeout is how one dead upstream host stalls a whole worker.
- **Write timeout.** How long to wait while pushing the request body out. Only
  matters for large uploads; for JSON APIs it is effectively never the problem.
- **Read timeout.** How long to wait between chunks of the response. This is the
  one people mean when they say "timeout". Note carefully that it is a gap
  timeout, not a total timeout: a server that dribbles one byte every second can
  keep a 5-second read timeout satisfied forever.
- **Pool timeout.** How long to wait for a free connection from the pool when
  every connection is already checked out. When a service degrades under load,
  pool timeouts are usually the first errors you see, and they are frequently
  misread as upstream failures. The upstream is fine; your pool is empty.

Because the read timeout is a gap timeout, a total deadline has to be enforced
separately, usually by wrapping the whole call in the runtime's own cancellation
primitive (in Python, `asyncio.timeout`). Any client library that offers only a
single scalar timeout cannot express "fail this request after 10 seconds no
matter what", and you should not pretend otherwise.

## Client-level versus request-level configuration

Timeouts are typically configurable at two scopes:

1. **Client level**, set once when the client is constructed. This becomes the
   default for every request the client issues.
2. **Request level**, passed to an individual call, overriding the client
   default for that call only.

The rule that keeps this manageable: set a conservative default at the client
level that is correct for the 95 percent case, and override at the request level
only for the specific calls you know are slow (a report endpoint, a bulk export,
an embedding batch). Sprinkling per-request timeouts everywhere produces a
codebase where nobody can answer "what is our timeout?".

A subtle trap: a request-level override usually replaces the entire timeout
configuration rather than merging with it. If the client default sets a 5-second
connect and 30-second read, and one call passes a bare `timeout=60`, that call
may now have a 60-second *connect* timeout as well. Pass a full timeout object,
not a scalar, when overriding.

## Connection pooling

The pool holds open connections keyed by (scheme, host, port). Two limits
matter:

- **Max connections**: the total number of sockets the client will hold open
  across all hosts. Set this near your concurrency ceiling, not above it.
- **Max keepalive connections**: how many idle connections stay open for reuse.
  Idle connections cost the remote server memory, and many load balancers close
  them unilaterally after 60 seconds, which surfaces in your logs as spurious
  read errors on the first request after an idle period.

Keepalive expiry should be set *below* whatever your upstream's idle timeout is.
If the load balancer closes at 60 seconds and your client expires at 90, you
will reliably hand a dead socket to one request in every idle cycle. Setting the
client's expiry to 20 or 30 seconds eliminates that class of error entirely.

## The client lifecycle mistake

The single most common performance bug: constructing a new client per request.
Doing so throws away the connection pool, so every request pays a full TCP and
TLS handshake, adding 50 to 200 milliseconds of pure latency and exhausting
ephemeral ports under load. Construct one client at application startup, hold it
for the process lifetime, and close it on shutdown.

In a framework with lifespan hooks, this means creating the client in the
startup handler, storing it on application state, and closing it in the shutdown
handler. Module-level construction also works but binds the client to import
time, which breaks under some test runners because the client captures the event
loop that existed at import.

## Retries

Retries belong above the transport, not inside it. A transport-level retry
cannot know whether your request was idempotent, and retrying a non-idempotent
POST is how duplicate records get created. The safe pattern is an explicit retry
wrapper that (a) only retries requests you have marked idempotent, (b) only
retries on connect errors, pool timeouts, and 5xx responses, never on 4xx, and
(c) applies exponential backoff with jitter, because synchronized retries from
many workers reproduce the original overload.

Cap total retry time against the caller's deadline. A three-attempt retry with
30-second timeouts turns a 30-second failure into a 90-second failure, which is
usually worse for the user than failing fast.

doc.title: vector-store-server-mode.md
doc.content:
# Running a Vector Store in Client-Server Mode

## Embedded versus client-server

Most vector databases ship two deployment shapes. In **embedded mode** the
database runs inside your process and writes to a local directory. In
**client-server mode** the database is a separate process (usually a container)
that your application talks to over HTTP.

Embedded mode is the right default for notebooks, tests, and single-process
scripts. It has no network hop, no separate deployment, and no version skew
between client and server. It has one disqualifying limitation for services: the
storage layer assumes a single writer. Two application workers pointed at the
same directory will corrupt the index, and the failure is silent for a while
before it becomes loud.

Client-server mode exists to solve exactly that. The server owns the storage; N
application workers are all clients. If your application runs more than one
process, and any web server running more than one worker does, you need
client-server mode. This is not a scale decision, it is a correctness decision.

## Configuring the client

A client needs a host, a port, and (in any deployment that is not your laptop)
an auth token. Ports are the usual source of confusion because the defaults
differ between the server's own documentation, the container image's exposed
port, and whatever your orchestration layer maps it to. Read the port from
configuration, never hard-code it in application code, and log the resolved
value once at startup so a misconfiguration is visible in the first ten lines of
your logs rather than in a stack trace an hour later.

Health-check before serving traffic. The client should issue a heartbeat call
during application startup and refuse to start if it fails. A service that
starts happily and then fails every request is much harder to diagnose than one
that refuses to start.

## Collections and metadata

A collection groups vectors of the same dimensionality with the same distance
metric. Two properties are fixed at creation and cannot be changed afterwards:

- **Dimensionality**, which is determined by your embedding model. Changing
  embedding models means creating a new collection and re-embedding everything.
  There is no migration path, because the old vectors are meaningless in the new
  model's space.
- **Distance metric**, usually cosine, inner product, or L2. Cosine is the right
  default for normalized text embeddings.

Every vector carries a metadata dictionary, and metadata filters are applied
*before* the nearest-neighbor search, not after. This matters for recall: if you
ask for the top 10 results with a filter that only 12 documents satisfy, you get
the 10 best of those 12, not the 10 best overall filtered down to nothing. Use
this deliberately. Filtering by source, version, or language is the cheapest
precision improvement available to a retrieval system.

Metadata values are typically restricted to scalars (string, int, float, bool).
Lists and nested objects are not supported by most engines. Encode a list as
either several boolean flags or a delimited string you match with a substring
filter, and accept that neither is elegant.

## Persistence and backups

In client-server mode, the server persists to a volume. Two operational facts:

1. The index is not a database you can safely copy while it is running. Snapshot
   the volume with the server stopped, or use whatever export API the engine
   provides.
2. Re-embedding is your real backup. Keep the source documents and the ingest
   pipeline reproducible, and treat the vector store as a derived artifact you
   can rebuild. Teams that treat the index as primary data eventually discover
   they cannot rebuild it, usually on the day they need to.

## Batch writes

Write in batches. Single-document writes pay per-call overhead on both the HTTP
hop and the index update. Batches of 100 to 500 documents are the usual sweet
spot; larger batches start hitting request size limits and make partial failures
harder to reason about.

Partial failure handling is worth designing before you need it. If a batch of
500 fails at document 300, most engines leave the first 300 written. Your ingest
loop needs to be idempotent (stable, content-derived IDs rather than random
ones) so that re-running it repairs the gap instead of duplicating work.

## Query latency

Approximate nearest-neighbor search is fast, but the HTTP hop and the embedding
call are usually not. In a typical retrieval request, embedding the query
dominates: 40 to 120 milliseconds for a hosted embedding API, against 5 to 20
milliseconds for the search itself. Optimizing the search before you have
measured the embedding call is a common misallocation of effort.

doc.title: testing-external-services.md
doc.content:
# Testing Code That Calls External Services

## The three testing strategies

Code that calls an external service can be tested three ways, and mixing them up
is why test suites become both slow and untrustworthy.

**Fake the boundary.** Replace the client object with a stand-in that returns
canned responses. Fast, deterministic, and completely blind to whether your real
request is well-formed. Fakes test your logic, never your integration.

**Intercept the transport.** Let your real client build a real request, but stop
it at the socket layer and return a recorded response. This catches malformed
URLs, wrong headers, and serialization bugs that fakes sail past. It is the best
default for the majority of tests against HTTP APIs.

**Hit the real thing.** Slow, flaky, requires credentials, and occasionally
costs money. Justified for a small number of contract tests that run on a
schedule rather than on every commit.

A healthy suite is roughly 80 percent transport interception, 15 percent fakes
for pure-logic paths, and a handful of real contract tests behind a marker that
CI runs nightly.

## Fixtures and scope

Test fixtures have a scope that controls how often they are built. Function
scope rebuilds per test and is the safe default. Session scope builds once for
the whole run and is what you want for anything expensive: a container, a
loaded model, a populated index.

The trap with session scope is shared mutable state. A session-scoped vector
store that one test writes to will change the behavior of a later test, and the
resulting failure appears only when tests run in a particular order, which is
the worst kind of failure to debug. The discipline: session-scoped fixtures may
be expensive, but they must be read-only, or they must expose an explicit reset
that every consuming test calls.

## Async tests

Async test functions need a plugin to run; the base test runner cannot await a
coroutine and will silently skip or warn on it depending on version. The failure
mode worth knowing: without the plugin configured, an async test that should
fail can report as passing, because the coroutine is created and never awaited.
Any suite with async tests should have one deliberately-failing async test
written once, run once, and then deleted, to prove the plugin is actually wired.

Event loop scope is the second async trap. If a session-scoped fixture creates
a resource bound to one event loop and each test runs on a fresh loop, every
test after the first fails with an obscure "attached to a different loop" error.
Either match the fixture's loop scope to the resource's, or build the resource
per test.

## Parametrization

Parametrization turns one test function into N test cases, each reported
separately. Use it for input tables: a list of (input, expected) pairs is far
more readable and far more debuggable than a loop with assertions inside,
because a loop stops at the first failure and reports one failure where there
were six.

Give parametrized cases explicit IDs. The auto-generated ones derived from the
argument values become unreadable as soon as your arguments are anything more
complex than short strings, and unreadable case names make CI output useless.

## Assertions on floating point

Never assert exact equality on floats that came out of a model, an embedding, or
any accumulation. Use an approximate comparison with an explicit tolerance. The
tolerance is a design decision you should write down: for cosine similarities,
1e-6 is usually far tighter than the thing you actually care about, and a
tolerance of 1e-3 with a comment explaining why is more honest.

For similarity scores specifically, prefer asserting on *ordering* rather than
on values. "The correct document ranks first" is a stable assertion that
survives an embedding model upgrade. "The score is 0.8412" is a test that will
break on a Tuesday for reasons unrelated to your code.

## Test data

Keep test fixtures small enough to read. A 20-document corpus you can hold in
your head catches more real bugs than a 10,000-document sample you cannot
inspect, because when the 20-document version fails you can immediately see
*why*. Save the large corpus for a separate, slower evaluation suite whose job
is measuring quality, not catching regressions.
